candidate_sources.title: Discula "Dogwood" Anthracnose [fact sheet] - UNH Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Dogwood anthracnose is caused by the fungal pathogen Discula destructiva. Initial foliar symptoms develop in May and June as brown spots with smoky, purple-brown margins on lower canopy branches, leading to dead leaves, twig dieback, and stem cankers. The fungus overwinters in diseased foliage and stem cankers, spreading via splashing water in wet weather. Management includes sanitation, pruning for air circulation, and fungicides at bud break.

candidate_sources.title: Dogwood Anthracnose : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Dogwood anthracnose, caused by Discula destructiva, was introduced into eastern North America from Asia in the late 1970s. Tan spots with irregular purple margins appear on leaves in the lower crown in spring. D. destructiva persists as cankers on trunks and branches; conidia formed in conidiomata are splashed by rain onto new growth. Cornus florida and C. nuttallii are susceptible while C. kousa, C. alternifolia and C. amomum are relatively resistant.

candidate_sources.title: Dogwood Anthracnose - Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES)
candidate_sources.snippet: Dogwood anthracnose is a destructive disease of flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) caused by the fungus Discula destructiva. Symptoms include leaf spots with purple margins, blotches, twig and branch dieback, cankers, and epicormic sprouts. Management focuses on sanitation, pruning, improving air circulation, and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Dogwood (Cornus spp.)-Anthracnose | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Dogwood anthracnose caused by Discula destructiva affects Cornus species including Pacific dogwood (C. nuttallii). Necrotic leaf lesions with reddish-purple borders, leaf blight, twig dieback, and trunk cankers develop. Includes cultural and chemical management recommendations for the Pacific Northwest.

candidate_sources.title: Dogwood Powdery Mildew (PPFS-OR-W-13) â€” University of Kentucky Plant Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Erysiphe pulchra (formerly Microsphaera pulchra) and Phyllactinia guttata can produce powdery mildew infections on dogwood. White powdery fungal growth is the distinguishing feature. Symptoms include reddish-brown or purplish blotches, yellowing, scorching, cupping and curling of leaves. Includes cultural, resistant-cultivar, and fungicide management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew on Dogwood â€” Tennessee State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: The disease is caused by the fungi Erysiphe pulchra and/or Phyllactinia guttata. The predominant pathogen in Tennessee, Erysiphe, overwinters as black spherical chasmothecia on leaf debris and releases ascospores in spring. Infection typically begins in early June and continues through September; high relative humidity favors disease.

candidate_sources.title: Dogwood Powdery Mildew: Signs and Symptoms | BYGL â€” Ohio State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: White powdery fungal growth is the distinguishing feature of dogwood powdery mildew. Symptoms on leaves include yellow patchy areas that become necrotic, reddish-brown or purplish blotches, scorching of tips and edges, cupping, curling, drooping and premature leaf fall. New growth is particularly susceptible.
